issues.item: Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'permanently humiliated' is hard to reconcile unless the illness involved a specifically shaming interpersonal circumstance; nothing else in the profile suggests that context. The other items center danger, fear, vivid reliving, and generalized threat, so humiliation stands out as clinically mismatched to the trauma type.

vignette:
Arthur, a 78-year-old retired database administrator, found himself seeking help after months of escalating distress following a severe bout of pneumonia. The illness had struck him suddenly a year and a half ago, escalating rapidly to critical care. He remembered the sterile, metallic tang of the hospital air, the antiseptic mingled with the faint, sickly-sweet scent of medications, as he fought for each breath, intubated and utterly dependent. That period, a blur of fear and helplessness, left an indelible mark.

Now, when Arthur remembers that frightening event, it feels like it is happening right now. The vividness of the hospital room, the sterile scent of antiseptic, and the terrifying sensation of fighting for breath are so real that he has come to believe his body is an enemy, constantly on the verge of betraying him again. He often finds these memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, pulling him back to the brink of suffocation and overwhelming horror. This intense reliving of his past suffering profoundly shapes his current worldview, leading him to feel that he has lost his faith in people, life, or a higher power, given how abruptly his health was taken from him.

Even within his quiet suburban home, Arthur feels a constant, pervasive sense of threat. He is superalert and watchful, perpetually on guard, scanning for anything amiss. This hypervigilance means he feels on guard even inside his own home, constantly checking the locks, listening intently to every creak and groan of the old house. This constant state of being superalert and watchful, especially when he is supposed to be safe in his own home, reinforces his conviction that the world is a dangerous place, where threats can emerge without warning, just as his illness did. He carries strong negative feelings such as fear and horror, a persistent undercurrent that makes relaxation impossible.

His once meticulous work as a database administrator, which he now does on a freelance basis from home, has suffered. The need for sustained concentration, crucial for debugging complex systems, is frequently interrupted by his internal vigilance. He finds himself checking his pulse, monitoring his breathing, and jumping at unexpected notifications from his computer, convinced they herald another crisis. This makes him fall behind on projects, eroding the sense of competence he once held dear. What frightens him most is this internal battle, the feeling that his body keeps reacting as if he is still in danger even when he is safe, a relentless alarm system that he cannot switch off. He understands intellectually that he is no longer in the ICU, but his senses, particularly the lingering olfactory recall of that hospital smell, and the visceral memories, tell a different story.

Arthur finally sought help, weary of the relentless internal battle. He longs for a sense of peace he hasn't known since before his illness, but he is terrified that this vigilance, this feeling of perpetual danger and betrayal by his own body, has become his permanent reality.
